learning.description: There are no pretrained numerical parameters. Demonstrations teach both episodic bindings and a symbolic quotient. Consolidation computes the additive subgroup of the integers generated by within-label translations; its generator is the gcd. The choice of anchor does not change the result. The gcd of differences from any fixed member of a label group equals the gcd of all pairwise differences within that group, and every member of the group has the same residue modulo that gcd. So g(E) and P(E) depend only on which records are retained, not on which retained record serves as a_y. The supported hypothesis class consists of a positive hidden period p and a one-to-one map from residue classes mod p to labels. This restriction matters: a periodic labeling that repeats a label on several residues need not be represented correctly. Compilation checks consistency with the stored demonstrations, but it does not certify extrapolation outside this class. All claims apply after COMMIT and before relevant episodes are evicted.
learning.few_shot_argument: Under the supported hypothesis class, every same-label difference is a multiple of the hidden period p, so the compiled gcd is a multiple of p. An incomplete set of generators therefore yields a finer quotient with some bindings missing. It never merges true residue classes, so it never produces a wrong point mass. Once the observed differences generate the whole subgroup pZ, the gcd equals p, and one observed label per residue determines the complete rule. The concrete protocol is as follows. Label the residue-0 class at anchor coordinate 0 and at the six coordinates p*m_i, i = 1..6, where each m_i is drawn independently and uniformly from 1..M. Then label residue r at coordinate r for r = 1..p-1. This uses p + 6 demonstrations, and M must satisfy p*M <= U. The gcd of the residue-0 group is p*gcd(m_1..m_6), and the other groups contribute only zero differences. Hence g = p exactly when gcd(m_1..m_6) = 1. For each prime q, P(q divides m_i) = floor(M/q)/M <= 1/q. A union bound over primes then gives probability at least 1 - sum_q q^-6 = 1 - 0.017070... = 0.98293 > 0.9829. If gcd(m) = h > 1, then g = p*h. The anchor residues 0..p-1 are distinct mod p*h, so the quotient is still valid. Positions whose residue mod p*h lies in 0..p-1 receive the correct label, and all other positions receive the uniform fallback. Generalization to every representable position then comes from executing the modulus, not from more examples. Sparse sampling without generator coverage is explicitly not guaranteed to identify the period.

readout.name: Exact episode, then quotient execution
readout.plain: Scan stored episodes newest-first for an exact coordinate match. If one is found, emit its label with probability one. Otherwise, if the compiled model is valid and has a label bound at this residue, emit that label with probability one. Otherwise emit the uniform distribution over the output labels Y. Represent the result exactly, as a point mass or as a uniform-support descriptor over Y; all other vocabulary tokens have probability zero.

state.meaning: The stream has n structured tokens z_t, for t from 1 through n. Each token is DEMO(x,y), QUERY(x) or COMMIT. Integer coordinates x lie in 0..U, where U is a fixed deployment bound; every claim in this card uses U = 100000. The label y belongs to the finite output-label set Y, a subset of a vocabulary of V tokens. Other vocabulary tokens receive zero output probability. B is a fixed positive consolidation interval; the toy uses B = 4. DEMO, QUERY and COMMIT are fixed parsing operations, not learned embeddings. The notation 1{condition}, the point mass delta_y and Unif(Y) have their usual meanings for discrete distributions. A QUERY requests one output-label token. A position with no query receives the same uniform fallback distribution.
state.name: Input specification

state.meaning: At most d records (x,y), ordered from oldest to newest; d is the episode capacity. The store starts empty. append_d appends a record and discards the oldest record if capacity is exceeded. E_y denotes the records currently in E with label y. a_y is the coordinate of the oldest record still retained in E_y. After an eviction, the anchor moves to the next-oldest surviving record with that label. At compilation, label groups are exact-address hard locations built with a temporary dictionary. J(E,x) is the label of the newest stored record at coordinate x, or the sentinel none if there is no such record.
state.name: E_t

state.meaning: g_t is the modulus, P_t is the residue-to-label dictionary and v_t is the consistency flag. The initial value is (0, empty, true). Define rho_g(x) = x when g = 0, and rho_g(x) = x mod g otherwise. For a store E, g(E) is the gcd of all differences |x - a_y| over records (x,y) in E. The gcd of an empty collection, or of only zeros, is 0. P(E) maps rho_{g(E)}(a_y) to y for each observed label y when there is no conflict. v(E) is true exactly when no two distinct labels have the same anchor residue; if v(E) is false, P(E) is empty. Compile(E) returns (g(E), P(E), v(E)). The modulus is learned structural state, not a trainable weight.
state.name: Q_t
shape: P_t: partial dictionary of at most d (residue -> label) pairs
state.type: Compiled symbolic model: tuple (g_t, P_t, v_t)

state.meaning: An integer in 0..B-1 that counts demonstrations since the last consolidation, modulo B. It starts at zero. COMMIT resets the clock and explicitly consolidates the current store. COMMIT marks the end of a demonstration block. It is part of the core interface, not an auxiliary training phase.
state.name: c_t

update.name: One-shot episode write
update.plain: On a demonstration, append its coordinate and label to the bounded ordered store. If the store already holds d records, evict the oldest. On any other token, leave the store unchanged.

update.name: Slow clock
update.plain: Increment the clock modulo B on each demonstration. Reset it to 0 on COMMIT. Otherwise leave it unchanged.

update.name: Translation subgroup generation
update.plain: Scan the store from oldest to newest and group records by label. The first record met for a label is its anchor a_y, which is the oldest retained record with that label. Fold each record's absolute difference from its anchor into a running gcd that starts at 0. Zero differences leave the gcd unchanged. If no difference is nonzero, the modulus is 0, which means no periodic generalization is inferred.

update.name: Quotient consistency and binding
update.plain: Insert one entry per observed label, mapping residue rho_g(a_y) to label y. If an insertion finds that residue already assigned to a different label, mark the compiled model invalid and discard the dictionary. Otherwise keep all entries. The pairwise condition in the definition is checked by dictionary insertion, not by a quadratic loop.

update.name: Consolidation commit
update.plain: Rebuild the modulus, the dictionary and the validity flag after every block of B demonstrations, or on COMMIT. Between rebuilds the compiled model stays unchanged, while stored episodes remain immediately available to the readout.

card.summary: This is a specialized sequence learner for periodic categorical rules, not a general language model. Its fast memory stores demonstrations exactly. Its slow learner treats two occurrences of the same label as evidence for an integer translation symmetry. It computes the subgroup generated by those translations and compiles a quotient lookup table. Predictions at new positions come from executing the quotient map, not from retrieving a similar episode. The central hypothesis is that the number of examples needed depends on whether the demonstrations generate the hidden symmetry subgroup, not on how many positions the rule covers. The gcd computation is classical. The proposed mechanism is its use as a consistency-checked consolidation step between episodic storage and next-token prediction.

toy_example.description: A complete bounded implementation (d = 8, B = 4). It shows immediate episodes, delayed consolidation, period-3 extrapolation, binding of the remaining residue, and invalidation after the conflicting demonstration (3,B). That demonstration adds the anchor difference |3-1| = 2, so the modulus becomes gcd(6,9,2) = 1. Anchors are the oldest retained record per label. Probability vectors list the three output-label coordinates; all other vocabulary tokens have zero probability.
toy_example.python:
import json
import math

class Learner:
    def __init__(self, capacity=8, batch=4):
        self.d = capacity
        self.B = batch
        self.E = []
        self.c = 0
        self.g = 0
        self.P = {}
        self.valid = True
        self.labels = [0, 1, 2]

    def rho(self, x):
        return x if self.g == 0 else x % self.g

    def compile(self):
        anchors = {}
        g = 0
        for x, y in self.E:
            if y not in anchors:
                anchors[y] = x
            g = math.gcd(g, abs(x - anchors[y]))
        self.g = g
        table = {}
        valid = True
        for y, a in anchors.items():
            r = self.rho(a)
            if r in table and table[r] != y:
                valid = False
            table[r] = y
        self.valid = valid
        self.P = table if valid else {}

    def demo(self, x, y):
        self.E.append((x, y))
        self.E = self.E[-self.d:]
        self.c = (self.c + 1) % self.B
        if self.c == 0:
            self.compile()

    def commit(self):
        self.c = 0
        self.compile()

    def query(self, x):
        chosen = None
        for a, y in reversed(self.E):
            if a == x:
                chosen = y
                break
        if chosen is None and self.valid:
            chosen = self.P.get(self.rho(x))
        if chosen is None:
            return [round(1.0 / len(self.labels), 6)] * len(self.labels)
        return [1.0 if y == chosen else 0.0 for y in self.labels]

m = Learner()
m.demo(0, 0)
m.demo(6, 0)
m.demo(1, 1)
before = m.query(3)
m.demo(10, 1)
after_first_commit = [m.query(3), m.query(7), m.query(2)]
m.demo(2, 2)
m.commit()
period = m.g
residues = sorted(m.P)
new_residue = m.query(5)
m.demo(3, 1)
m.commit()
result = {
    'before': before,
    'after_first_commit': after_first_commit,
    'period': period,
    'compiled_residues': residues,
    'new_residue': new_residue,
    'conflict_valid': m.valid,
    'conflict_exact': m.query(3),
    'conflict_unseen': m.query(11),
    'episodic_size': len(m.E)
}
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

critic.mapping:
The card has two parts. Both map onto known constructions with no residue left over.

(1) Fast store E_t and readout J(E_t,x) form an exact-match hard-attention cache over a sliding window of the last d DEMO tokens.
- key_i = x_i, value_i = onehot(y_i), query = x.
- score_i = 1{x_i = x}, with ties broken by recency.
- Output is argmax-attention onto value_i, or 'none'.
- append_d with oldest-first eviction is exactly a length-d sliding window over DEMO tokens.

(2) Compiler Compile(E) is the classical most-specific-consistent-lattice learner for integer lattices (Helmbold, Sloan & Warmuth, 'Learning Integer Lattices', 1992), specialized to dimension 1 and wrapped in a multiclass coset table.
- The within-label differences x - a_y are the positive examples of the unknown subgroup pZ.
- g(E) = gcd of those differences is the Hermite normal form, i.e. the generator, of the smallest subgroup L = gZ containing them. This is HSW's closure step; in 1-D the HNF is the gcd.
- Each label y is the coset a_y + L.
- P(E) is the coset-to-label table rho_g(a_y) -> y.
- v(E) is the consistency test that distinct labels occupy disjoint cosets.
- The 'finer quotient never merges classes' guarantee is the standard property of the most specific hypothesis: L is contained in the true lattice, so pZ ⊇ gZ and g is a multiple of p.
- Uniform fallback is abstention on an unbound coset.
- The B-clock and COMMIT only schedule when the closure is recomputed.
- The 1/zeta(6) sample-efficiency figure is the textbook probability that six random integers are coprime, i.e. that they generate Z.

So the per-token update is: push into a bounded FIFO, and periodically recompute a gcd closure. The readout is: exact cache hit, else coset lookup, else abstain.
critic.textbook_why: The card's stated sources are SDM hard-location storage and CLS fast/slow consolidation, and it changes both substantially. SDM is cut down to an exact-address FIFO cache with no counters or similarity readout. The CLS slow learner is replaced outright by a gcd/coset compiler. The compiler itself (gcd closure of differences, i.e. 1-D integer-lattice learning) is used exactly as textbook number theory and Helmbold–Sloan–Warmuth state it. So the novelty is in the recombination, not in any change to a construction.
critic.why:
This is not a renamed recurrence, SSM or linear attention. There is no affine state update, kernel accumulation or learned readout, so those reductions fail. However, the core mechanism is a known symbolic learner:
- The fast path is a hard exact-match cache over a window of d demos.
- The slow path computes the smallest integer subgroup containing same-label differences and binds labels to its cosets. This is the most-specific-consistent-lattice algorithm from computational learning theory, in one dimension, where it is just gcd.
- The headline sample-efficiency result, 1/zeta(6), is the classical coprimality probability.
- The hypothesis class is hand-restricted to bijective periodic labelings, with no learned parameters and no path to general sequence modeling.

A researcher familiar with grammatical or lattice inference and with program-synthesis-style version spaces would not be surprised. It is a known algorithm placed inside a CLS-flavored interface, which the gate treats as a transplant rather than a radical mechanism. The prior-art search found no exact paper, but that reflects the narrowness of the combination, not novelty of the mechanism.

Setup: m = 64, d = 256, s = 2. Store 128 random atoms (one DEMO each). Present 100 demonstrations of random consistent pairs DEMO({a, b}, v_a + v_b). Then present 100 inconsistent ones with value v_a + v_b + 1. The store never exceeds 228 <= d, so nothing is evicted.

Predictions:

- All 100 inconsistent composites are written.
- Each inconsistent composite, queried again immediately, is answered with its demonstrated value at accuracy >= 0.99.

The last prediction holds because its stored key equals the query and so has the Cauchy-Schwarz-maximal normalized score ||q||, about 1.41, against about 1 for each atom. It is selected first, with zero residual.

Setup: m = 64, d = 256, s = 2, 128 stored atoms. Query 100 distinct three-cue composites {a, b, c}; the target is v_a + v_b + v_c.

Predictions:
- Accuracy <= 0.3 before any demonstration, because only two atoms can be selected.
- After one DEMO of each such composite, repeating the same queries gives accuracy >= 0.99. Each DEMO is always written, because a three-cue key is generically not 2-sparse in the store. After all 100 writes the store holds 228 <= d episodes, so nothing is evicted.

Why the repaired query is answered correctly: the stored composite key equals the query q = k_a + k_b + k_c, so its normalized score is exactly ||q|| = sqrt(3 + 2(k_a.k_b + k_a.k_c + k_b.k_c)). This is the Cauchy-Schwarz maximum, about 1.73 for these codes. Each atom scores about 1, and a stored composite sharing two cues scores about 2/sqrt(3) = 1.15. The exact composite is therefore selected first, with zero residual.

complexity.constants_notes:
Per-step cost:
- Scoring: at most s passes over at most d stored keys, each one m-dimensional dot product (cached key norms).
- Refit: a pseudoinverse solve on at most s columns, O(s^2 m).
- Key: O(w m) for the key sum.
- Write: O(m + p).

Readout: O(V p) to materialize all logits, or O(p) per token if only the argmax (nearest output code) is needed.

Memory is d(m + p + 1) numbers plus the parameter block, with p <= m.

All claims use s = 2. Nothing grows with n: the store is capped at d.

known_relatives.claimed_difference:
Their state is a function of G = sum k k^T and H = sum k y^T, or of an order-weighted version, and their readout is linear in the query, so they realize a map of rank <= m.

learning.description:
In context, the only learning is the one-shot gated write u4. The store is a dictionary of episodes grown only by unexplained data.

Slowly, theta = (C, E, beta) can be pretrained on many synthetic in-context sequences by minimizing next-token cross-entropy. During this training:
- the support S_t from u2 is treated as a constant;
- gradients flow through the least-squares solution alpha_t = pinv(K_{S_t}) k_t into C, and through yhat_t into E.
Pretraining should lower the mutual coherence of the codes, which enlarges the recoverable sparsity.

All claims below are stated for the untrained instance (random unit Gaussian codes, E[y] = y). The claims test the mechanism, not the training.

equations.latex: \mathcal L(\theta)=-\sum_{t:z_t=\mathrm{DEMO}}\log p_t(y_t),\quad \nabla_\theta \text{ through } \alpha_t=K_{S_t}^{+}k_t \text{ with } S_t \text{ held fixed}
equations.name: pretraining loss
equations.plain: Cross-entropy of the label at each DEMO step. Backpropagate through the least-squares coefficients on the selected support; the selection itself is held fixed.

learning.few_shot_argument:
A binding shown once is written in one shot. A new random key is generically not in the span of any s stored keys, so its pursuit residual is nonzero.

Now take a later query whose key equals an s-sparse signed combination of stored keys, k_q = sum_{i in T} c_i K_i with |T| <= s. Once the pursuit selects exactly T, the refit gives alpha = c with zero residual, and yhat = sum_i c_i v_i. This is exactly the value under an additive binding rule, whether or not this combination was ever shown.

When is T selected? The worst-case guarantee ((2s-1) mu < 1, with mu the mutual coherence) does NOT hold in the claimed setup. For 256 random unit codes in R^64, mu is about 0.6. The claims instead rest on a per-query estimate. For a non-support unit key k_i, k_i . u is approximately N(0, ||u||^2 / m).

Pair query q = k_a + k_b, with rho = k_a . k_b:
- Step 1: each support key scores 1 + rho, while a non-support key scores about N(0, (2 + 2 rho)/m). The margin is z = sqrt(m (1 + rho)/2), which is about 5.7 at m = 64 and rho = 0. The per-key exceedance probability is about 1e-8, and the union over 254 keys is about 1e-5 (about 3e-4 at a 2-sigma rho = -0.25).
- Step 2: the residual is k_b - rho k_a. The true key scores 1 - rho^2, the others score about N(0, (1 - rho^2)/m), and z = sqrt(m (1 - rho^2)), about 8.

Inferred binding (query k_b with stored composite k_a + k_b and atom k_a):
- Step 1: the composite scores 1/sqrt(2), about 0.71, against noise of std 1/8 (z about 5.7).
- Step 2: the residual is about (k_b - k_a)/2. The atom k_a scores 0.5 against noise of std about 0.088 (z about 5.7).

Consequences:
- d one-shot atoms answer on the order of d^s composites.
- A cue never shown alone (b) is answered from one composite (a+b) and one atom (a), because k_b = 1*(k_a + k_b) - 1*k_a is 2-sparse in the store.

The novelty gate keeps explained composites out of the store, so the d slots hold independent information.

Capacity is limited. At most d episodes are retained under FIFO eviction. Composites needing more than s atoms are answered wrongly until one demonstration of them is written.

readout.name: next-token distribution
readout.plain:
For every output token v, the logit is -beta * squared distance between its output code E[v] and yhat_t. Apply a softmax over the V tokens.

On DEMO steps this is the prediction made before y_t is revealed; on QUERY steps it is the answer. With E[y] = y, the argmax is the integer token nearest to yhat_t.

state.name: Input specification

state.meaning:
C[x] in R^m is the cue code of cue token x (one row per cue token, U rows), and m is the key dimension. E[y] in R^p is the output code of output token y (one row per output token, V rows), and p is the value dimension. beta is the readout inverse temperature.

The claims use an untrained instance:
- U = 256 cue tokens; rows of C are i.i.d. Gaussian, normalized to unit length;
- V = 64 output tokens 0..63, p = 1 and E[y] = y.

Pretraining (see learning) adapts C and E for natural data.
state.name: theta = (C, E, beta)

state.meaning:
Column i of K_t is the key of a stored episode, and column i of Y_t is its value code. The norm ||K_i|| is cached when the episode is written. The store starts empty.

append_d(M, (k, v)) appends a column pair and drops the oldest pair if the size would exceed d. K_S denotes the columns of K indexed by an ordered index list S, and Y_S likewise for Y.
state.name: M_t = (K_t, Y_t)
state.type: Bounded episodic store, ordered oldest to newest

state.meaning: S_t is the selected support. alpha_t holds the minimum-norm least-squares coefficients on K_{S_t}. r_t = k_t - K_{S_t} alpha_t is the unexplained residual of the query key. yhat_t = Y_{S_t} alpha_t is the predicted value code. yhat_t is the zero vector when S_t is empty.
state.name: (S_t, alpha_t, r_t, yhat_t)
shape: S_t: ordered list of <= s store indices
state.type: Pursuit result at step t (temporary, recomputed every step)

update.name: u1: cortical key
update.plain: k_t = sum of the cue codes C[x] over the nonempty cue set X_t of the current step.

update.latex: r^{(0)}=k_t,\ S^{(0)}=\varnothing;\ \text{for } j=1..s:\ i_j=\arg\max_{i\notin S^{(j-1)}}\frac{|K_{t-1,i}^\top r^{(j-1)}|}{\|K_{t-1,i}\|};\ \text{stop if the max}\le\tau;\ S^{(j)}=S^{(j-1)}\cup\{i_j\},\ \alpha^{(j)}=K_{t-1,S^{(j)}}^{+}\,k_t,\ r^{(j)}=k_t-K_{t-1,S^{(j)}}\alpha^{(j)}
update.name: u2: explaining-away pursuit
update.plain:
Start with residual r = k_t and an empty support. Repeat up to s times:
1. Over stored episodes not yet selected, compute |K_i . r| / ||K_i||. Take the largest, breaking ties by the lowest index.
2. If it is <= tau, stop.
3. Otherwise add that index to the support.
4. Re-solve least squares for k_t on all selected keys, taking the minimum-norm solution alpha = pinv(K_S) k_t (numpy.linalg.lstsq).
5. Set r = k_t minus the fitted combination.
The final support, coefficients and residual are S_t, alpha_t and r_t.

Linear dependence: r is orthogonal to span(K_S) after every refit. A stored key lying in that span therefore scores exactly 0 and is never selected. The pseudoinverse keeps step 4 defined if near-dependent keys are selected numerically. Generic random codes give full column rank, where pinv(K_S) k_t = (K_S^T K_S)^{-1} K_S^T k_t.

update.name: u3: value inference
update.plain: The predicted value code is the same signed combination of the selected stored values: yhat_t = sum_j alpha_t[j] * Y[:, S_t[j]]. Coefficients may be negative.

update.name: u4: novelty-gated one-shot write
update.plain: On a demonstration, store (k_t, E[y_t]) only if the pursuit failed to explain it: either the key residual norm exceeds eps, or the predicted value differs from the true value code by more than eps. If the store is full, drop the oldest episode. Explained demonstrations and queries leave the store unchanged.

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant:
The parent's mapping relies on two properties:
(i) retrieval is exact match (score 1{x_i = x}) or a lookup in a table derived from an order-independent closure of positive examples;
(ii) the learned structure is the most specific hypothesis containing the observed differences.

In this card, neither holds:
- u2-u3 answer a query whose key matches no stored key with a signed combination sum_j alpha_j Y_{i_j}. The support is chosen by residual correlation after earlier selections (explaining away), and the coefficients come from a joint least-squares refit.
- u4 writes an episode only if that pursuit fails, so the store's contents depend on the solve and on write order. 'a+c -> 8' is dropped after atoms a and c are stored, but it would be stored if shown first.

The neighbouring numeric families share a further invariant: their state is a function of G = sum k k^T and H = sum k y^T (or a decay-weighted version), and their readout is linear in q. Both properties fail here. The readout is piecewise linear in q, with a data-chosen support. It is not invariant under the index rotation (K, Y) -> (KQ, YQ), which preserves G and H exactly. The toy prints 3.0 vs -0.65812 for two stores with identical G and H.
non_reduction_argument.known_family: other_known: exact-match hard-attention cache over a sliding window plus the Helmbold-Sloan-Warmuth most-specific integer-lattice (gcd/HNF closure) learner with a coset-to-label table
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable:
Exact cache: the query 'b' has no stored key, so any exact-match cache returns none. There is no closure or HNF step, and the hypothesis class is additive binding over learned codes, not a lattice.

Strongest numeric repair: MesaNet / RLS / delta rule with a learned feature map phi. Its readout H^T (G + lambda I)^{-1} phi(q) is linear in phi(q).
- Explaining away requires phi(k_b) = phi(k_a + k_b) - phi(k_a) for every stored pair. So phi must be additive on the code lattice, that is, linear on span(C), and so of rank <= m.
- The fitted map then has rank <= m and cannot reproduce d > m generic bindings (capability 1).
- A non-additive phi loses explaining away (capability 2).
- Larger lifted states do not help: any state that is a function of (G, H) gives identical outputs for the toy's stores X and Y, while the core gives different ones.

Strongest attention or kernel repair: multi-hop softmax or Hopfield retrieval. Its weights f(k_i, q)/Z are nonnegative, computed per item, and independent of values. The correct answer v_{a+b} - v_a depends with coefficient -1 on an item whose key is nearly orthogonal to the query. Swap v_a with the value of another unrelated stored item: the true answer changes by their difference, but any kernel readout changes only by about |f(k_a, q) - f(k_j, q)|, which is close to 0.

An attend-subtract-reattend stack would have to compute the least-squares refit pinv(K_S) q on a data-chosen support and gate writes on its residual. That is this mechanism, not a member of the family. Its failure would show up on capabilities 2 and 3.

references.why: Supplies the SDM read rule (pool the contents of the hard locations activated by an address). Also supplies the result that SDM capacity can grow independently of the stored-vector dimension, which motivates the overcomplete regime d > m that this card targets. The radius activation is replaced by pursuit activation.

Surveys distributed memories that store more items than their dimension, and bipartite networks that recall by iterative residual correction under linear constraints. The pursuit read is a residual-correcting recall carried out directly over stored episodes.

CTDL writes its hippocampal store when the slow system's error is high (CLS fast/slow split). Here the error gate becomes the store's own sparse-explanation residual, and pretrained cue codes play the slow cortical role.

source_transplant.change:
Three changes to the SDM rule:
- The activated set is chosen by s-step orthogonal matching pursuit on the query residual, not by a Hamming radius.
- Contents are pooled with signed least-squares coefficients, not counter sums.
- Hard locations are allocated on demand as one-shot episodes, not as fixed random addresses.

The CTDL write gate uses the pursuit's key and value residual instead of a TD error, so the same solve both reads and decides what to write.
source_transplant.object: The Kanerva SDM read rule (pool the contents of the hard locations an address activates; capacity beyond the vector dimension), together with CTDL's error-gated write to the hippocampal store

card.summary:
The fast store is a bounded set of episodes (key, value). Keys come from slow, pretrained cue codes; in CLS terms these are the cortical representations.

Retrieval does not look up the most similar episode. It runs s steps of orthogonal matching pursuit over the stored keys. Each step:
- picks the stored key most correlated with the current residual of the query;
- re-fits least-squares coefficients on the keys picked so far;
- subtracts their contribution from the query.
The answer is the same signed combination of the stored values.

A query that matches no stored episode can therefore be answered by inference. Suppose the store holds 'a+b -> 7' and 'a -> 3'. Then the query 'b' resolves to 7 - 3 = 4. This is explaining away: the stored atom a enters with coefficient -1 even though its key is orthogonal to the query.

Writes are gated by the same solve. A demonstration is stored only if the pursuit cannot reproduce both its key and its value. Composites that are consistent with stored atoms are therefore never stored, and capacity goes to genuinely new bindings.

The store may hold more episodes (d) than the key dimension (m). This follows the SDM point that capacity can exceed the vector dimension. Any memory whose readout is linear in the query can realize only a rank-m map, so it cannot exploit this regime.

Cost is O(s d m) per token, with no growth in n.
card.title: Explaining-Away Episodic Store: sparse-pursuit recall with novelty-gated one-shot writes

toy_example.description:
Part 1 uses m = 3, s = 2, d = 8, cue codes a, b, c = unit basis vectors, and E[y] = y.
- Demonstrations, in order: a+b -> 7, a -> 3, c -> 5, a+c -> 8, b+c -> 9.
- 'b' is never shown alone; it is inferred as 7 - 3 = 4.
- 'a+c -> 8' is explained by the stored atoms, so it is not written.
- 'b+c' is 3-sparse in the store at that point, so the s = 2 pursuit predicts 8.5. Its demonstration is therefore written, after which the same query returns 9.

Part 2 builds two stores in R^2 with identical G = sum k k^T and H = sum k v^T (the program's variables GX/GY and CX/CY hold G and H). Store Y is store X with its first two episodes rotated by an orthogonal mixing. The pursuit readout of query e1 differs (3.0 vs -0.65812), while the in-context least-squares readout H^T G^{-1} q is 0.9456 for both. No function of (G, H) can reproduce the core readout.

numpy.linalg.lstsq returns the minimum-norm least-squares solution, which is the pseudoinverse refit of u2. The score test against tau matches u2.
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np

def omp(q, keys, s, tau=1e-9):
    S, alpha, r = [], np.zeros(0), q.copy()
    for _ in range(s):
        best, bi = tau, -1
        for i, k in enumerate(keys):
            if i in S:
                continue
            c = abs(float(k @ r)) / float(np.linalg.norm(k))
            if c > best:
                best, bi = c, i
        if bi < 0:
            break
        S.append(bi)
        K = np.stack([keys[i] for i in S], axis=1)
        alpha = np.linalg.lstsq(K, q, rcond=None)[0]
        r = q - K @ alpha
    return S, alpha, r

def read(keys, vals, q, s=2):
    S, a, r = omp(q, keys, s)
    y = float(sum(a[j] * vals[i] for j, i in enumerate(S))) if S else 0.0
    return y, r

class Store:
    def __init__(self, d=8, s=2, eps=1e-6):
        self.d, self.s, self.eps = d, s, eps
        self.K, self.Y = [], []
    def predict(self, q):
        return read(self.K, self.Y, q, self.s)
    def demo(self, q, v):
        y, r = self.predict(q)
        wrote = bool(np.linalg.norm(r) > self.eps or abs(v - y) > self.eps)
        if wrote:
            self.K.append(q)
            self.Y.append(float(v))
            if len(self.K) > self.d:
                self.K.pop(0)
                self.Y.pop(0)
        return wrote, y

def token(yhat, beta=2.0, V=16):
    logits = [-beta * (v - yhat) ** 2 for v in range(V)]
    return int(np.argmax(logits))

C = {'a': np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 'b': np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), 'c': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])}
def key(cues):
    return sum(C[x] for x in cues)

m = Store()
w = []
r1, _ = m.demo(key('ab'), 7); w.append(r1)
r2, p_a = m.demo(key('a'), 3); w.append(r2)
qb, _ = m.predict(key('b'))
r3, _ = m.demo(key('c'), 5); w.append(r3)
r4, p_ac = m.demo(key('ac'), 8); w.append(r4)
bc0, _ = m.predict(key('bc'))
r5, _ = m.demo(key('bc'), 9); w.append(r5)
bc1, _ = m.predict(key('bc'))

KX = [np.array([1.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.96, 0.28])]
VX = [3.0, 5.0, 0.0]
cs, sn = 0.8, 0.6
KY = [cs * KX[0] + sn * KX[1], -sn * KX[0] + cs * KX[1], KX[2]]
VY = [cs * VX[0] + sn * VX[1], -sn * VX[0] + cs * VX[1], VX[2]]

def gram(K, V):
    G = sum(np.outer(k, k) for k in K)
    Cv = sum(k * v for k, v in zip(K, V))
    return G, Cv

GX, CX = gram(KX, VX)
GY, CY = gram(KY, VY)
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
mesaX = float(CX @ np.linalg.solve(GX, q))
mesaY = float(CY @ np.linalg.solve(GY, q))
ompX, _ = read(KX, VX, q)
ompY, _ = read(KY, VY, q)
gc = float(max(np.max(np.abs(GX - GY)), np.max(np.abs(CX - CY))))

result = {
    'wrote': w,
    'pred_a_demo': round(p_a, 6),
    'query_b': round(qb, 6),
    'query_b_token': token(qb),
    'pred_ac_demo': round(p_ac, 6),
    'query_bc_before': round(bc0, 6),
    'query_bc_after': round(bc1, 6),
    'query_bc_after_token': token(bc1),
    'store_size': len(m.K),
    'X_omp': round(ompX, 6),
    'Y_omp': round(ompY, 6),
    'X_mesa': round(mesaX, 6),
    'Y_mesa': round(mesaY, 6),
    'GC_maxdiff': round(gc, 6)
}
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

critic.difference_if_any:
What remains is a combination of known parts, not a new update.
- The ALD/RAN admission test uses the s-sparse OMP residual instead of the dense projection residual or nearest-centre distance.
- The coupled dictionary holds raw episodes from an in-context token stream instead of image patches or training samples.
- Eviction is FIFO.

The read is textbook OMP plus coupled-dictionary code transfer. The write is error- and novelty-gated exemplar allocation. Swapping the sparse residual into an ALD/RAN-style test is a modest variant, not a new learning rule.
critic.mapping:
Exemplar-dictionary coupled sparse coding (Yang, Wright, Huang & Ma, 'Image super-resolution as sparse representation of raw image patches', CVPR 2008; also sparse-representation regression and classification over raw training samples, Wright et al. SRC) with greedy OMP as the solver. Its dictionary grows by a novelty and error allocation rule in the style of Platt's Resource-Allocating Network (1991) and Engel's ALD sparsification, here tested on the s-sparse residual.

Symbol map:
- K_t (stored keys) = the low-resolution / input dictionary D_l, whose atoms are raw stored exemplars, not learned atoms.
- Y_t (stored values) = the coupled high-resolution / output dictionary D_h. Column i of D_h is paired with column i of D_l.
- u1, k_t = sum C[x] = the input signal to be coded. C is a fixed random (or pretrained) feature map.
- u2 = textbook OMP with sparsity s on D_l. It picks argmax |<d_i, r>| / ||d_i||, re-solves least squares on the support, and updates the residual. The card itself says 'u2 is OMP used unchanged'.
- u3, yhat = Y_S alpha = the coupled-dictionary reconstruction x_h = D_h alpha. The sparse code from the input dictionary is transferred unchanged to the output dictionary.
- u4 = RAN/ALD-style allocation. Add the exemplar (k_t, E[y_t]) as a new dictionary pair when the current approximation leaves key residual > eps or output error > eps. ALD uses the dense projection residual, RAN uses nearest-centre novelty together with error. Here the residual is the s-sparse OMP residual, and either condition triggers a write.
- append_d = a budgeted dictionary with FIFO removal (budgeted kernel/online learners).
- Readout p_t = a Gaussian-distance softmax over output codes, i.e. nearest-integer decoding.
- Pretraining through alpha = K_S^+ k with S fixed = the standard task-driven dictionary learning gradient (Mairal, Bach & Ponce 2012), which differentiates through the support-restricted least-squares code.
critic.textbook_why: The stated source construction is Kanerva SDM (Hamming-radius activation, counter-sum pooling, fixed random hard locations) together with CTDL's TD-error-gated write. The card replaces all three SDM elements with OMP selection, signed least-squares pooling and on-demand allocation, and replaces the TD gate with a pursuit residual. So the stated source construction is materially changed, even though the replacement components are themselves textbook OMP and coupled-dictionary coding.
critic.why:
Escape test, parent mapping: the argument holds.
- u2-u3 do answer non-matching queries with signed least-squares combinations, so retrieval is not exact-match.
- u4 makes store contents order-dependent, so there is no gcd/HNF closure.
- The card's further invariant is also correct. A readout that is piecewise linear on a data-chosen support is not a function of (G, H). The toy's rotation counterexample is valid.
- The MesaNet, RLS and delta-rule repairs fail for the stated rank reason.
- Softmax and Hopfield repairs fail because explaining away needs a coefficient of -1 on a near-orthogonal key. I checked the inferred-binding margins: step 1 scores about 0.71 against noise of about 0.125; step 2 scores 0.5 against about 0.088. The 2-sparse solve then gives exactly (1, -1).
- So the card does not reduce to the parent's cache-plus-lattice learner, nor to linear attention, SSM, RNN or kernel memory.

Closest repair, which succeeds as a reduction to other_known: coupled-dictionary sparse coding over raw exemplar pairs. Sparse-code the input on dictionary D_l and reuse the code on D_h. This is exactly OMP-on-keys followed by alpha-on-values. Add a RAN/ALD-style rule that admits only unexplained samples.
- Yang et al. 2008 even uses raw sampled patch pairs as the dictionary, with signed sparse codes.
- Overcompleteness (d > m), negative coefficients and sparse-recovery capacity are the standard selling points of that literature. They are not new here.
- The card's own known_relatives concedes that OMP is unchanged and that KRLS-ALD gates admission the same way, differing only in dense versus sparse residual.

Why not radical: a researcher who knows sparse coding, super-resolution coupled dictionaries and resource-allocating networks would recognize the mechanism immediately. Moving it into a token-stream memory is a transplant, not a new mechanism.

capabilities.prediction: Top-1 accuracy >= 0.95 and mean probability on the correct value >= 0.8. Accuracy changes by at most 0.02 when 0 to 4000 filler tokens are inserted. The precondition, checked directly on the trained model, is that all filler-involving pairs have K0 <= kappa = 1e-3. In that case filler bigrams are never imprinted and cannot evict key-value imprints, and the 32 filler right species add at most 32 * kappa = 0.032 to any key's denominator 1 + (K y)_q.
capabilities.task: One-shot associative recall: the sequence k1 v1 k2 v2 ... k8 v8 followed by a query k_i. 8 random keys from tokens 0-31, 8 random values from tokens 32-95, V = 128, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3. Variant: 0 to 4000 filler tokens from 96-127 are inserted before the query.

capabilities.prediction: The held-out value is the top-1 prediction in >= 90% of trials, and its mean probability over trials is >= 0.30. Row-local ablation on the same trained model (same E, F, beta and imprint table): p_loc(v) = K[q,v] / sum_{v': a[v']=1} K[q,v'], over tokens present in context, which is what a count cache or one-hot linear-attention readout gives. The query key's row has no imprints, so p_loc(v) = K0[q,v]/sum K0[q,.] over the 8 inventory values, up to keys present with K0 <= kappa. Under a random bijection the held-out value is uniform over the inventory and independent of q's prior row, so E[p_loc(held-out)] = 1/8 exactly. The measured mean over 1000 trials is predicted to lie in 1/8 ± 0.02. The gap between the mean model probability and the mean row-local probability is >= 0.15, and it comes only from the conservation coupling.
capabilities.task: Elimination (mutual exclusivity): the context lists an inventory of m = 8 value tokens, then demonstrates 7 of the 8 pairs of a random bijection between 8 keys and the 8 values, then queries the 8th key, which was never demonstrated. 1000 trials with fresh random keys, values and bijections.

capabilities.prediction: At convergence the bound parts satisfy exactly C_qa/C_qb = (K0_qa/K0_qb) e^{beta (k_a - k_b)} y_a/y_b. With no other binder, y_v = 1/(1 + K_qv x_q), so log(C_qa/C_qb) is strictly increasing in k_a - k_b. Each unit step changes it by an amount in (0, beta]. The step equals beta in the weak-binding limit K_qv x_q << 1 and is compressed under saturation. Measurable: with K0_qa/K0_qb in [0.8, 1.25], p(a) > p(b) in >= 95% of trials with k_a > k_b, and every measured unit-step increment of log(C_qa/C_qb) lies in [0, beta + 0.05].
capabilities.task: Graded conflicting evidence: key q is shown with value a k_a times and with value b k_b times (k_a + k_b <= 4). No other key in context binds a or b.

capabilities.prediction: For K <= 16, accuracy >= 0.9. For K = 32, eviction (smallest count, ties broken by least recent increment) keeps only the last 16 imprints, so overall accuracy is 0.5 ± 0.1. The last 16 pairs score >= 0.9. The first 16 score <= 0.1, because each evicted key spreads its mass over the roughly 16 values left free, which is the elimination effect at chance. A fixed state cannot hold more than P_max one-shot bindings.
capabilities.task: Capacity limit: one-shot recall of K = 8, 16 or 32 pairs with P_max = 16 (other settings as in the first task). Value->key bridge pairs have K0 <= kappa, so each key-value pair uses exactly one imprint.

complexity.constants_notes: Each sweep costs O(V r) for E(F^T y) and F(E^T x), plus O(P_max) for the sparse correction over the imprint table, where each record caches K0_ij, computed in O(r) at insertion. The gate test and the minimum-count eviction scan cost O(r + P_max) per token. Each token runs J warm-started sweep pairs, and the claims take J = 3 as a fixed constant, so the true cost is about 2 J (2 V r + P_max). The readout row K[q,:] costs O(V r), the same order as an LM output projection of width r. x, y and a take 3V memory, and the table takes 5 P_max numbers. Nothing depends on n, because the table has at most P_max records. Training with implicit differentiation adds a CG solve of at most 50 iterations, each with a matvec costing O(V r + P_max). The initial state is x_0 = y_0 = a_0 = 0 with an empty table.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: The gated imprint e^beta on K_ij plus re-equilibration. One demonstration of a binding shifts the equilibrium enough to dominate the readout, with no test-time gradient step. Pretraining only learns the role prior E F^T (which token types bind), the scalar beta and the background u. It never learns the bindings themselves.

prediction.metric: In-context exposures per new key-value pair needed to reach top-1 recall >= 0.95. Setup: K = 8 pairs per sequence, V = 128 split into keys 0-31, values 32-95 and filler 96-127, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3, measured on 1000 held-out sequences with fresh random pairings.
prediction.statement: One demonstration of each pair gives top-1 recall >= 0.95 and mean p(correct) >= 0.8, which matches the first capability claim. Pretraining protocol: one pass over synthetic recall sequences with fresh random pairings, Adam with learning rate 1e-2 and batch 32, and held-out recall evaluated every 100 sequences. Secondary prediction: the median over 5 seeds of the number of pretraining sequences seen before held-out one-shot recall first reaches 0.95 is <= 3000. This is plausible because only 2Vr + V + 1 parameters are trained and no binding is stored in weights.

card.core_idea: Each observed adjacent token pair (i, j) lowers the standard free energy of a complex C_ij in a reversible binding network X_i + Y_j <-> C_ij, whose species totals are set by which tokens are present in context; the next-token distribution is the bound fraction of the current token's species at the network's unique detailed-balanced equilibrium (the Birch point), so competing bindings deplete each other through conservation laws.

extensions.description: Replace the unit totals with learned per-token capacities s^L_i and s^R_j, so that function words can bind many successors. This relaxes the one-to-one bias of the core for natural text. The sweeps stay the same, with a replaced by a ⊙ s.

equations.latex: x \leftarrow (a \odot s^L) \oslash (\mathbf{1} + K y),\quad y \leftarrow (a \odot s^R) \oslash (\mathbf{1} + K^{\top} x)

extensions.name: Learned stoichiometric capacities

extensions.description: Following finite stochastic CRN semantics (W2008591003), use small integer molecule counts and sample the stationary distribution of the binding network. At unit counts this gives exact discrete matchings instead of fractional bindings, which is useful for strict permutation tasks.
extensions.name: Finite-count stochastic regime

extensions.description: Add reactions X_i + Z_k + Y_j <-> C_ikj, imprinted by triples (w_{t-2}, w_{t-1}, w_t), with their own capped repertoire. This conditions bindings on a two-token context, for example 'relation r applied to key k'. Conservation still couples all complexes through the shared totals.
extensions.name: Trimolecular complexes for two-token contexts

falsifiers: On the elimination task (m = 8, 7 pairs shown, inventory listed, 1000 trials), the mean probability the trained model gives the held-out value exceeds the mean row-local ablation probability (p_loc(v) = K[q,v]/sum over present tokens of K[q,.], with the same E, F, beta and imprint table) by less than 0.15. That would show the conservation coupling adds nothing.

One-shot associative recall with K = 8 pairs (V = 128, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3) fails to reach top-1 accuracy 0.95, the threshold of the first capability claim, with one exposure per pair after pretraining, but reaches it with two or more. That would refute the claim that a single e^beta imprint plus re-equilibration is enough.
With V, r and P_max fixed, measured time per token grows by more than 10% when context length goes from n = 1,000 to n = 64,000. That would refute the n-independent cost claim.

With J = 3 warm-started sweep pairs per token, the readout differs from the fully converged Birch-point readout by total variation distance > 0.05 on more than 5% of recall-task positions. In that case the constant J in the cost claim does not hold, and the true cost includes a growing convergence factor.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The readout is not a linear or row-local function of the state. It is the minimizer of a convex free energy under per-token conservation laws, and that minimizer couples every row to every column. p(v | q) depends on how strongly other keys bind v. This is why elimination works. A row-local readout of the same affinities gives an undemonstrated key's held-out value exactly 1/m in expectation over random bijections, whatever the prior row.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention (Transformers are RNNs) / count-based cache language models
known_relatives.relation: The imprint update N_t = N_{t-1} + gate * e_{w_{t-1}} e_{w_t}^T is an additive outer-product accumulator with one-hot features. It is the state update of linear attention or a bigram cache (an S_t = S_{t-1} + B x_t form), and we say so plainly.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those methods scale an n x n position-by-position attention matrix, which is quadratic in n. Here the scaled matrix is a token-type by token-type affinity whose context-dependent part has at most P_max entries. The transport is unbalanced: the free monomers x and y absorb unmatched mass, and that free fraction is the fallback to u. The equilibrium constants are written by gated in-context co-occurrence, not by query-key dot products.
known_relatives.name: Sinkhorn / optimal-transport attention (doubly stochastic attention normalization)
known_relatives.relation: Matrix scaling of a positive kernel to prescribed marginals is the same mathematics as the binding equilibrium with conserved totals. Entropic OT is a special case of Birch's theorem.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those models have no conserved quantities and no global equilibrium readout. Their state decays and is gated, so no conservation law forces bindings to compete. Here nothing decays. Capacity is a hard cap on distinct complexes with eviction, and inference is constrained free-energy minimization.
known_relatives.name: Mamba / RWKV / RetNet / xLSTM
known_relatives.relation: Linear-time recurrent sequence models with fixed-size state.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Here competition is not a heuristic normalization. It is the exact equilibrium of a detailed-balanced mass-action network, with a uniqueness guarantee (the Birch point), a convex objective, and a closed-form implicit gradient. The mixing weight on the background u is the free concentration x_q, which the chemistry determines. It is not a learned gate.
known_relatives.name: Cross-situational word-learning models with competition (mutual exclusivity) and pointer-sentinel mixtures
known_relatives.relation: Psychology models of word-object mapping use competition between candidate mappings. Pointer-sentinel models mix a copy distribution with a background distribution.

learning.description: E_raw, F_raw, b and l are trained by next-token cross-entropy on pretraining sequences. There are two equivalent options. (1) Backpropagate through the J unrolled sweep pairs. (2) Differentiate through the converged Birch point by the implicit-function theorem, using the closed form below. On the support of a_t, use log coordinates sigma = log x and tau = log y. The Hessian of G in (sigma, tau) at the equilibrium is H = [[Id, C], [C^T, Id]], where Id is the identity matrix on the support and C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j. The diagonal blocks are Id because x_i(1 + (Ky)_i) = a_i = 1 there. H is symmetric positive definite because G is strictly convex in (sigma, tau). The adjoint system H [lambda; mu] = [x ⊙ dL/dx; y ⊙ dL/dy] is solved by conjugate gradients. CG starts from lambda = mu = 0 and stops when the residual norm is at most 1e-6 times the norm of the right-hand side, or after 50 iterations, whichever comes first. Each matvec C z costs O(V r + P_max). The gradient with respect to K is a rank-2 dense term plus sparse parts, so it is never materialized. It is pushed to E, F and beta through K = K0 ⊙ exp(beta N). Nothing is updated by gradient at test time. All in-context adaptation is the imprint table plus re-equilibration.

equations.latex: G(x,y) = \sum_{i: a_t[i]=1} (x_i - a_t[i]\log x_i) + \sum_{j: a_t[j]=1} (y_j - a_t[j] \log y_j) + \sum_{ij} K_t[i,j]\, x_i y_j,\quad (x^*,y^*) = \arg\min_{x,y>0} G
equations.name: free energy whose minimizer is the readout state
equations.plain: Setting the gradient of G to zero gives exactly x_i = a_t[i]/(1 + (K y)_i) and y_j = a_t[j]/(1 + (K^T x)_j). G is strictly convex in (sigma, tau) = (log x, log y) on the support of a_t, so the minimizer is unique and the alternating sweeps (exact block minimization) converge to it. Off the support, x_i = y_j = 0.

equations.name: training loss
equations.plain: loss = - sum over positions t of log p_t[w_{t+1}].

equations.latex: \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{Id} & C \\ C^{\top} & \mathrm{Id} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\ \mu\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x\odot \partial_x \mathcal{L} \\ y \odot \partial_y \mathcal{L}\end{pmatrix},\quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K_{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K_{ij}}\Big|_{\text{explicit}} - (\lambda_i + \mu_j)\, x_i y_j
equations.name: implicit gradient through the Birch point
equations.plain: Solve for lambda and mu by CG on the support of a_t (initial guess 0, stop at relative residual <= 1e-6 or 50 iterations), with C z = x ⊙ (K (y ⊙ z)) and C^T z = y ⊙ (K^T (x ⊙ z)). Then dL/dK[i,j] = explicit_ij - (lambda[i] + mu[j]) * x[i] * y[j], where explicit_qv = (dL/dp[v]) * x[q] * y[v] for the readout row q and 0 elsewhere. Chain rule: dK[i,j]/dE[i,k] = F[j,k] * exp(beta*N[i,j]), dK[i,j]/dF[j,k] = E[i,k] * exp(beta*N[i,j]), dK[i,j]/dbeta = N[i,j] * K[i,j]. So dL/dE is the rank-2 dense part -((x⊙lambda) y^T + x (y⊙mu)^T) times F, plus row q and the sparse corrections on S_t.

learning.few_shot_argument: One exposure of a gated pair (i, j) (K0_ij > kappa) multiplies K_ij by e^beta, a learned free-energy drop. At the new Birch point, the complex C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j takes most of X_i's unit total as soon as e^beta K0_ij is large compared with the competing terms in 1 + (K y)_i. So one demonstration is enough for recall. k demonstrations give an affinity K0_ij e^{k beta}, so conflicting evidence enters the equilibrium constants multiplicatively. The conservation law y_j + sum_i C_ij = a_j makes the readout of key q depend on every other key's bindings. A value bound strongly elsewhere has a small free concentration y_j, so the probability of an undemonstrated key moves to the values that are still free. This is how a rule shown for m-1 of m items determines the m-th. The inference is done by chemical equilibration (free-energy minimization within the stoichiometric class). It is neither a gradient step nor a stored lookup.

readout.latex: p_t(v) = K_t[q,v]\, x_q\, y_v + x_q\, u_v, \quad q = w_t,\; u = \mathrm{softmax}(l)
readout.name: bound-plus-free fraction of the current token's left species
readout.plain: p[v] = K[q,v]*x[q]*y[v] + x[q]*u[v], with q the current token and u = softmax(l). The last x sweep sets x[q] = 1/(1 + Ky[q]) and a[q] = 1, and u sums to 1, so sum_v p[v] = x[q]*(Ky[q] + 1) = 1 exactly, even before full convergence.

state.meaning: Phi is the column concatenation of two V x r blocks. V is the vocabulary size and r is the prior rank. E = Phi[:, :r] and F = Phi[:, r:] each have shape V x r, so the block has 2Vr numbers. They give the prior equilibrium constants K0 = E F^T >= 0 between left species X_i and right species Y_j. This is the pretrained notion of which token types can bind which, for example keys binding values. Pairs with K0_ij <= kappa (a fixed constant, kappa = 1e-3) are treated as non-binding and are never imprinted.
state.name: Phi = [E | F]
state.type: learned parameter block, nonnegative (E = softplus(E_raw), F = softplus(F_raw))

state.meaning: The imprint free energy is beta = softplus(b) > 0, so each imprint multiplies K_ij by e^beta. The background distribution is u = softmax(l), a point in the probability simplex over V tokens. It receives the unbound fraction of the current token's left species. Only b and l are stored. beta and u are always computed from them.
state.name: (b, l)
state.type: learned parameters: scalar b and logit vector l

state.meaning: N_t is stored only as this table. The notation N_t[i,j] means the count of the record (i, j) if one exists, and 0 otherwise. In other words, N_t is the logical V x V matrix that is zero off the table and is never materialized. N_t[i,j] counts how often token j directly followed token i with K0_ij > kappa. S_t = {(i,j): N_t[i,j] > 0} is the set of stored pairs, with |S_t| <= P_max. P_max is the number of distinct complex species the reaction volume holds, a fixed size independent of n. last_increment_step is used to break eviction ties. cached K0_ij is computed in O(r) when the record is created. N_0 is empty.
state.name: N_t (imprint table)
state.type: sparse table of at most P_max records (i, j, count, last_increment_step, cached K0_ij)

state.meaning: a_t[i] = 1 if token i has occurred in w_1..w_t, else 0, with a_0 = 0. It is the conserved total of both X_i and Y_i, and it is the same a_t that appears in the free energy G. Tokens that are absent contribute no species.
state.name: a_t

state.meaning: x_t[i] is the free (unbound) concentration of X_i at the current equilibrium estimate, with 0 <= x_t[i] <= a_t[i] and x_0 = 0. A newly injected species starts fully free (x[i] = 1).
state.name: x_t

state.meaning: y_t[j] is the free concentration of Y_j at the current equilibrium estimate, with 0 <= y_t[j] <= a_t[j] and y_0 = 0. A newly injected species starts at y[j] = 1. A small y_j means value j is already consumed by other bindings.
state.name: y_t

update.name: gated imprint with capped complex repertoire
update.plain: if t >= 2 and dot(E[w_{t-1}], F[w_t]) > kappa: if a record (w_{t-1}, w_t) exists, increment its count and set last_increment_step = t; otherwise create it with count 1, last_increment_step = t, and cached K0. If the table now holds more than P_max records, delete the record with the smallest count, breaking ties by the smallest last_increment_step. Pairs at or below kappa (for example filler bigrams or value->key bridges, which have near-zero prior affinity) never enter the table, so they cannot evict real bindings.

update.name: species injection (new mass enters free)
update.plain: if a[w_t] == 0: a[w_t] = 1; x[w_t] = 1; y[w_t] = 1. All other entries are unchanged. Together with x_0 = y_0 = a_0 = 0, this fixes the warm start of the sweeps at every t, including t = 1.

update.latex: K_t = (E F^{\top}) \odot \exp(\beta N_t),\quad (K_t y)_i = E_i^{\top}(F^{\top} y) + \sum_{j:(i,j)\in S_t} K^0_{ij}\,(e^{\beta N_t[i,j]}-1)\, y_j
update.name: context-written equilibrium constants (never materialized)
update.plain: Ky = E @ (F.T @ y); then for each record (i,j) in the table: Ky[i] += K0[i,j]*(exp(beta*N[i,j]) - 1)*y[j]. Likewise KTx = F @ (E.T @ x); for each record (i,j): KTx[j] += K0[i,j]*(exp(beta*N[i,j]) - 1)*x[i]. A row or column with no record receives no correction. K0[i,j] is read from the record's cache.

update.name: free right-species sweep
update.plain: for each j: y[j] = a[j] / (1 + KTx[j]). This is exact minimization of G over log y with x fixed.

update.name: free left-species sweep (alternates with the y sweep, J times per token)
update.plain: for each i: x[i] = a[i] / (1 + Ky[i]). The pair (y sweep, then x sweep) runs J times per token, where J is a fixed integer (J = 3 in all claims). It starts from the warm start given by the previous token and the injection step. The fixed point is the unique Birch point C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j with x_i + sum_j C_ij = a_i and y_j + sum_i C_ij = a_j.

references.why: Source of the central object. Detailed-balanced chemical reaction networks have product-form mass-action equilibria (generalized Boltzmann machines), and conservation laws condition those equilibria. I take the binding equilibrium C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j under conserved totals, together with its free-energy characterization, and use it as the inference step of a sequence learner whose equilibrium constants are written by the context.

Finite stochastic CRN semantics with integer molecule counts. It is used only in the 'finite-count stochastic regime' extension, where the deterministic Birch point is replaced by the stationary distribution of a finite-count network. The core does not depend on it.

source_transplant.change: In chemistry the equilibrium constants are fixed. Here the context writes them. Each observed adjacent pair with prior affinity above a threshold multiplies K_ij by e^beta, starting from a learned low-rank prior E F^T. Species totals are injected when a token occurs. The equilibrium is tracked by warm-started alternating sweeps instead of being simulated in time. The bound and free fractions of the current token's left species are read out as a next-token distribution.
source_transplant.object: The detailed-balanced mass-action equilibrium of reversible binding reactions X_i + Y_j <-> C_ij with equilibrium constants K_ij and stoichiometric conservation laws: C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j, with x_i + sum_j C_ij = total_i and y_j + sum_i C_ij = total_j. It is the unique positive equilibrium in its compatibility class (the Birch point) and the minimizer of the Gibbs free energy. The cited paper identifies it as a product-form equilibrium, a generalized Boltzmann machine whose conservation laws condition the distribution.

card.summary: Tokens are species. The first time a token i occurs, one unit of a 'left' species X_i and one unit of a 'right' species Y_i are injected, and both start out free. Each observed adjacent pair (w_{t-1}, w_t) whose learned prior affinity exceeds a fixed threshold kappa multiplies the equilibrium constant of the reversible reaction X_{w_{t-1}} + Y_{w_t} <-> C_{w_{t-1} w_t} by e^beta. The constants start from a learned low-rank nonnegative prior K0 = E F^T. The model holds the mass-action, detailed-balanced equilibrium of this binding network. That equilibrium is unique in each stoichiometric compatibility class (Birch's theorem). It minimizes a convex free energy and is found by warm-started alternating fixed-point sweeps on the free concentrations x and y. The prediction after token q is the vector of complexes C_qv, plus the free fraction x_q routed to a learned background distribution u. Every value species has a total of 1 that all keys share, so the readout is not row-local. A value already bound strongly by another key is depleted, which pushes a never-demonstrated key toward the values that are still free. This is elimination, or mutual-exclusivity inference. A per-row normalization of the same affinities gives the held-out value only 1/m in expectation. The state is a sparse imprint table capped at P_max gated entries plus O(V) concentrations, so cost per token does not depend on n. Training differentiates through the equilibrium in closed form. In log coordinates, the Hessian of the free energy at the Birch point is [[Id, C], [C^T, Id]], where C is the complex matrix.
card.title: Birch-Point Binding Chemistry: in-context bindings as the mass-action equilibrium of a reversible binding network under conservation laws

toy_example.description: Six tokens: keys 0, 1, 2 and values 3, 4, 5. The role prior K0 = E F^T with r = 1 lets only keys (left species) bind values (right species), each with K0 = 1. E and F are set directly to their post-softplus values, using exact zeros as the limiting case. The sequence [5, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2] first shows value 5 (inventory), then the pairs (0 -> 3) and (1 -> 4), then the query key 2, which was never paired. The bridge pairs (5,0), (3,1) and (4,2) have K0 = 0 <= kappa, so the gate does not imprint them. beta = ln 9, so demonstrated pairs have K = 9. All mass starts free (x = y = a, the injection rule). Alternating sweeps run to convergence. By uniqueness of the Birch point, this equals the per-token warm-started procedure run to convergence. The equilibrium is x = y = 1/4 for the demonstrated keys and values and 1/2 for key 2 and value 5. Key 2's bound mass therefore goes twice as much to the still-free value 5 as to each depleted value (elimination). Its free fraction of 1/2 goes to the uniform background over values. The row-local baseline is uniform (1/3 each).
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
V = 6
E = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0], dtype=float).reshape(V, 1)
F = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float).reshape(V, 1)
K0 = E @ F.T
kappa = 1e-3
beta = np.log(9.0)
u = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float) / 3.0
seq = [5, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2]
N = np.zeros((V, V))
a = np.zeros(V)
prev = None
for w in seq:
    if prev is not None and K0[prev, w] > kappa:
        N[prev, w] += 1.0
    a[w] = 1.0
    prev = w
K = K0 * np.exp(beta * N)
x = a.copy()
y = a.copy()
for _ in range(500):
    y = a / (1.0 + K.T @ x)
    x = a / (1.0 + K @ y)
def readout(q):
    return K[q] * x[q] * y + x[q] * u
p2 = readout(2)
p0 = readout(0)
r = lambda v: [round(float(t), 4) for t in v]
out = {
    "x_free_keys": r(x[:3]),
    "p_q2_values": r(p2[3:]),
    "p_q0_values": r(p0[3:]),
    "rowlocal_q2": r(K[2, 3:] / K[2, 3:].sum()),
    "rowlocal_q0": r(K[0, 3:] / K[0, 3:].sum()),
    "argmax_q2": int(np.argmax(p2)),
    "mass_q2": round(float(p2.sum()), 4)
}
print(json.dumps(out))

critic.difference_if_any: The normalization is over token types, not over positions. The card scales a V x V type-by-type kernel whose context part is a capped sparse count table. It does not scale an n x n position matrix, so cost is independent of n. The marginals are binary presence indicators, and the dustbin potential is pinned to 1 rather than given a fixed marginal. The equilibrium is tracked incrementally with J warm-started sweeps per token. The column-coupling effect (elimination / mutual exclusivity) is precisely what Sinkhorn normalization adds over row-softmax, and it is known in OT matching (SuperGlue's one-to-one assignment bias). The learning rule (cross-entropy with BPTT or implicit differentiation through the scaling fixed point) is not new.
critic.mapping: Update: N_t = N_{t-1} + gate * e_{w_{t-1}} e_{w_t}^T is the linear-attention state S_t = S_{t-1} + phi(k_t) v_t^T. Here phi(k_t) = e_{w_{t-1}} and v_t = e_{w_t} are one-hot, and a binary gate 1[K0 > kappa] is applied. This is a gated bigram/count cache, and the card concedes it. The P_max cap with min-count eviction is a fixed-size LFU cache over the same outer-product state. The effective kernel K = (E F^T) ⊙ exp(beta N) is a low-rank learned bilinear prior times an exponentiated count cache. That is a kernel over token types, with log K_ij = log(E_i·F_j) + beta N_ij acting as the 'attention logit'. Readout: the fixed point x_i = a_i/(1+(Ky)_i), y_j = a_j/(1+(K^T x)_j) is alternating Sinkhorn/matrix scaling of the kernel K to marginals a. P_ij = x_i K_ij y_j is the transport plan with row potential x and column potential y. The '+1' terms are a dustbin row and column with kernel entry 1 whose scaling is pinned at 1. This is exactly SuperGlue-style unbalanced Sinkhorn with slack: the free monomer is the dustbin mass. The readout p(v) = P_qv/a_q + x_q u_v takes row q of a Sinkhorn-normalized kernel and sends the dustbin mass to a learned background distribution, as a pointer-sentinel mixture does. Taken together, the card is Sinkhorn (doubly stochastic, OT) normalized attention (Sinkformer / Sparse Sinkhorn / SuperGlue dustbin) applied to a vocabulary-indexed one-hot linear-attention/bigram-cache state. Training through the fixed point by implicit differentiation is standard differentiable Sinkhorn (Hessian [[Id, C],[C^T, Id]] in log-potentials).
critic.textbook_why: The core object is the textbook detailed-balanced mass-action equilibrium of reversible binding reactions under conservation laws (the Birch point, the Gibbs free-energy minimizer). It is computed by the standard alternating fixed point, and the card does not change its equations. The card's changes are only in the inputs: equilibrium constants written by a gated count of token bigrams on top of a learned low-rank prior, and totals set by token presence. It then adds a next-token readout with a background distribution. The construction itself is unmodified.
critic.why: The state update is a gated, capped one-hot outer-product accumulator, which is linear attention or a bigram cache. The card says so itself. The only non-standard part is the readout, and that is matrix scaling of a positive kernel to prescribed marginals with slack.
